stdout_tail:
**Finding (H1): yes, model family matters — but with a low ceiling.**

Seven families, ROC-AUC on an untouched 30% test set (n=14,653):

| Model | Test AUC | Acc | AP |
|---|---|---|---|
| Hist gradient boosting | **0.9315** | 0.874 | 0.836 |
| Random forest | 0.9207 | 0.868 | 0.814 |
| MLP (64,32) | 0.9152 | 0.858 | 0.787 |
| Decision tree | 0.9084 | 0.857 | 0.780 |
| Logistic regression | 0.9083 | 0.855 | 0.771 |
| k-NN | 0.8705 | 0.840 | 0.665 |
| Gaussian NB | 0.8625 | 0.752 | 0.659 |

Two things are true at once. The spread is real and statistically overwhelming — 0.069 AUC best-to-worst, ~13× the largest within-family fold sd (0.0054), with boosting winning 15/15 paired CV folds against every comparator. But it's bounded: five of seven families sit inside 0.908–0.932, and the best model beats a plain L2 logistic regression by only **+0.023 AUC**. So the choice buys you a couple of AUC points, not a different class of predictor. The families that genuinely lag (naive Bayes, k-NN) fail for identifiable reasons — NB's independence assumption on one-hot columns, k-NN's distance metric in ~90-dim one-hot space.

**Verification.** Paired bootstrap on the test set (2,000 resamples): HGB − LogReg +0.0232 [+0.0207, +0.0257], HGB − GaussianNB +0.0689 [+0.0638, +0.0742] — all CIs exclude zero. Independently, 3×5 repeated stratified CV over all 48,842 rows with a different seed reproduced it almost exactly: spread 0.0654 (vs 0.0690), boosting-over-logistic gap 0.0229 (vs 0.0232). The finding held.

**Choices another researcher might make differently:** dropped `fnlwgt` (a sampling weight) and the redundant `education` string; `?` → explicit "Missing" level rather than dropped rows; per-family encoding (one-hot+scaling for linear/distance/neural, ordinal/native-categorical for trees) rather than one uniform encoder; equal-budget small hyperparameter grids tuned inside the training split only; ROC-AUC primary with no imbalance reweighting. XGBoost/LightGBM weren't installed, so the top of the range could move slightly with a stronger booster.

Files written: `analysis.py`, `result.json`, plus `analysis_details.json` with the full per-model numbers.

parsed_result.summary: Yes, but modestly. Across seven model families the held-out ROC-AUC spans 0.863 (Gaussian naive Bayes) to 0.932 (histogram gradient boosting) - a 0.069 spread, roughly 25x the within-model fold-to-fold noise, so family choice is real and statistically unambiguous. The effect is nonetheless bounded: every family except naive Bayes and k-NN lands in a narrow 0.908-0.932 band, and gradient boosting beats a plain L2 logistic regression by only 0.023 AUC (0.932 vs 0.908), so the practical payoff from picking the best family over a competent linear baseline is a couple of AUC points, not a difference in kind.
parsed_result.primary_metric_name: Held-out ROC-AUC spread across model families (best - worst: HistGradientBoosting - GaussianNB)
parsed_result.direction: Model family matters but with a modest ceiling: HistGradientBoosting > RandomForest > MLP > LogReg ~= DecisionTree > k-NN > GaussianNB; boosting beats logistic regression by only +0.023 AUC
parsed_result.methodological_choices: Target = P(class '>50K'), 23.9% prevalence. Dropped fnlwgt (census sampling weight, not a person-level feature) and the string `education` column (exactly redundant with education-num). '?' values parse as NaN and were mapped to an explicit 'Missing' category for the three affected columns (workclass, occupation, native-country) rather than dropped, since missingness is informative here. 52 exact duplicate rows were left in. Encoding was per-family rather than uniform: one-hot (min_frequency=10) + standardization for logistic regression, Gaussian NB, k-NN and the MLP; ordinal codes for decision tree / random forest / HistGradientBoosting (with native categorical handling for HGB) - i.e. each family got the representation it would normally be given in practice. Families compared: majority-class dummy, GaussianNB, k-NN, single decision tree, L2 logistic regression, random forest (500 trees), HistGradientBoosting (300 iters), MLP (64,32) with early stopping. Light and deliberately equal-budget hyperparameter tuning (2-8 candidates per family) by 3-fold CV inside the training split only. Primary metric ROC-AUC because it is threshold-free and insensitive to the 76/24 imbalance; accuracy, balanced accuracy, average precision and F1@0.5 also reported and give the same ranking. No class-imbalance reweighting or resampling was applied (it does not change a ranking based on ROC-AUC/AP, but it would change the F1@0.5 column). Evaluation: stratified 70/30 split, all tuning confined to the 70%. Notably, richer alternatives another researcher might pick (XGBoost/LightGBM, target encoding, deeper nets, threshold tuning) were not tried - XGBoost was unavailable in this environment - so the top of the range could shift by a small amount.
parsed_result.verification_method: Two independent checks. (1) Paired bootstrap on the untouched 30% test set (n=14,653; 2,000 resamples, same resampled rows for both models) for the key AUC differences. (2) A fully separate 3x5 repeated stratified cross-validation over all 48,842 rows using a different random seed (777) from the split-based analysis, with hyperparameters frozen at the values chosen on the training split; because all families see identical folds, per-fold differences are paired and were tested with a paired t-statistic and a win count.
parsed_result.verification_result: Held up, with essentially unchanged estimates. Repeated CV gives HistGradientBoosting 0.9293 +/- 0.0026, RandomForest 0.9197 +/- 0.0025, MLP 0.9130 +/- 0.0035, LogisticRegression 0.9064 +/- 0.0041, DecisionTree 0.9054 +/- 0.0031, k-NN 0.8674 +/- 0.0041, GaussianNB 0.8638 +/- 0.0054. Best-worst spread 0.0654 (vs 0.0690 on the single split) and the boosting-vs-logistic gap 0.0229 (vs 0.0232). Test-set paired bootstrap 95% CIs exclude zero for every comparison: HGB - GaussianNB +0.0689 [+0.0638, +0.0742], HGB - LogReg +0.0232 [+0.0207, +0.0257], LogReg - GaussianNB +0.0458 [+0.0412, +0.0505]. Per-fold paired differences: HGB beat LogReg in 15/15 folds (+0.0229, t=43.0), beat RandomForest in 15/15 (+0.0096, t=49.2), beat GaussianNB in 15/15 (+0.0654, t=50.9). Maximum within-family fold sd is 0.0054, so the between-family spread is about 12-25x the run-to-run noise. Best estimate of the primary metric: ROC-AUC spread 0.065-0.069 across families; boosting-over-logistic gap 0.021-0.026.

supporting_results.note: Full per-model detail, bootstrap CIs and repeated-CV output are in analysis_details.json; code in analysis.py.
